To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the visibility of a visual stimulus is determined by the local state of visual cortex and by the global pre stimulus connectivity pattern, and that the latter is reflected by the peak latency of TMS evoked potentials.

(1) pre stimulus TMS applied to the frontal cortex can induce visual masking; (2) the individual extent of pre stimulus masking is highly correlated with the peak latency of a TMS evoked response; (3) the latter finding is consistent with a global connectivity view of pre stimulus masking.

1) pre stimulus TMS applied to the frontal cortex can disrupt the processing of a subsequent stimulus; 2) the effect is subject specific and correlates with a subject s peak latency of a TMS evoked late positive potential; and 3) the individual peak latency of this late positive potential is correlated with the individual peak latency and amplitude of a TMS induced late positive potential.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interplay between the local and global state of the visual cortex in visual masking and the role of TMS in the investigation of such processes.
the neural correlates of visual masking.
the neural basis of visual masking.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pre stimulus cortical state, as well as the connectivity patterns, are crucial factors for the subsequent visual information processing.
the visibility of a visual stimulus is determined by the local state of early visual areas, global connectivity patterns, and individual differences in cortical excitability.
TMS can be used as a tool for investigating the functional connectivity of the brain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pre stimulus masking effects depend not only on the local state in the early visual cortex, but also on the global connectivity pattern between early visual cortex and frontal areas.
TMS can be used to induce masking effects even in the absence of direct interactions with the visual cortex.

the effect of a TMS pulse on the subsequent processing of a visual target is not determined by the location of the pulse alone but rather by the interaction of local cortical states with global connectivity patterns.
The main takeaway from our work is that

individual variability in TMS effects should be considered in the future and that the individual peak latency of a TMS evoked late positive component could be a promising candidate to predict the individual extent of TMS induced visual masking.
TMS induced effects can be highly subject specific.
the TMS evoked potentials are a valuable tool for the characterization of inter individual differences in the TMS response.
